answer.evidence: I scanned every layer-1 unit. Most (0, 3-7, 9-16, 19, 21, 22, 24-26, 28, 30, 31) look like initialisation noise: values spread roughly ±60-80 with no spatial structure, and none contains a small cluster of out-of-range weights such as a corner or edge patch. The structured units fall into two groups. (1) Centre-weighted blobs. Units 18, 20 and 29 have positive weights over rows ~6-19 and cols ~5-18, reaching 80-99. Units 1 and 8 are positive over a broad central-to-wide area. Pushing each through W2 and W3 gives clearly positive net logit effects: unit 18 ≈ +3.2e4, unit 1 ≈ +1.8e4, unit 20 ≈ +1.1e4, unit 8 ≈ +9.6e3 (integer-product units), and unit 29 is only weakly positive (≈ +700). (2) Surround/ring units. Unit 17 is positive in the top rows 0-6, the bottom rows 22-23 and the right columns, and negative in the centre rows 8-17. Unit 23 is positive along top rows 0-3 (row sums ≈ +600 to +830, versus about 0 for other rows) and bottom rows 21-23. Unit 27 is positive over the periphery and negative in the lower centre. Their net output effects disagree in sign: unit 23 ≈ -6.0e3, unit 17 ≈ -2.4e3, unit 27 ≈ +6.0e3. These units span the whole periphery rather than one compact patch. Their top/bottom concentration is the closest thing to a shortcut candidate, but it is not a compact patch and the units do not agree on direction, so I read them as context (surround versus centre contrast) features. No small, compact image region gets consistently large weights across several units that then feed the output in one direction, which is the signature of an artifact shortcut.
answer.main_feature: The model mainly responds to bright, dense tissue in the central region where the nodule sits (larger or denser central opacity pushes toward malignant). Several units also contrast the centre against the surrounding lung and periphery.
